period: Often regarded as one of the latest principal Upanishads, perhaps around the turn of the Common Era; dating is uncertain
summary: Twelve short prose statements that map the syllable Om onto waking, dream, deep sleep and a fourth state (turiya) identified with the Self.
whyRead: The shortest principal Upanishad, it offers a complete map of consciousness in a few lines, using experience everyone has (waking, dreaming, dreamless sleep) as the starting point for inquiry. Through Gaudapada's Karika on it, it became a foundation of Advaita.
questions: What is common to waking, dreaming and deep sleep?
Is there consciousness beyond these states?

keyTeachings.title: All this is Om
keyTeachings.text: The text opens by identifying the syllable Om with everything, past, present and future, and with what lies beyond time.

keyTeachings.title: This Self is Brahman
keyTeachings.text: It states that all this is Brahman and that the Self is Brahman, one of the classical 'great sayings' (mahavakyas).

keyTeachings.title: Four quarters of the Self
keyTeachings.text: The Self is described in four aspects: the waking (vaishvanara), the dreaming (taijasa), the deeply sleeping (prajna), and the fourth (turiya), which is none of these.

keyTeachings.title: The fourth
keyTeachings.text: Turiya is described only by negation: not inwardly or outwardly conscious, not graspable, peaceful and non-dual. Advaita treats it as the Self underlying all three states.

keyTeachings.title: Om as a map
keyTeachings.text: The sounds A, U and M are matched to the three states, and the silence after the syllable to the fourth.

passages.about: All this is Brahman; this Self is Brahman
The parts of Om matched to the states of consciousness

relatedTexts.note: Gaudapada's verse commentary, the earliest surviving Advaita treatise, is built on this Upanishad
Its discussion of Om and sleep anticipates Mandukya's scheme
Contains earlier Upanishadic reflections on dream and deep sleep
